claim: Compulsive behaviors, characteristic of obsessive-compulsive disorder and addiction, are theorized to be driven by shared deficits in goal-directed control.
source: Prominent theories suggest that compulsive behaviors, characteristic of obsessive-compulsive disorder and addiction, are driven by shared deficits in goal-directed control, which confers vulnerability for developing rigid habits.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to theoretical frameworks in the literature.

claim: Deficient goal-directed control accompanies several psychiatric disorders, including those without an obvious compulsive element.
source: However, recent studies have shown that deficient goal-directed control accompanies several disorders, including those without an obvious compulsive element.
evidence: This claim references recent studies showing this pattern.

claim: Deficits in goal-directed control were most strongly associated with a symptom dimension comprising compulsive behavior and intrusive thought.
source: Using large-scale online assessment of psychiatric symptoms and neurocognitive performance in two independent general-population samples, we found that deficits in goal-directed control were most strongly associated with a symptom dimension comprising compulsive behavior and intrusive thought.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from two independent samples analyzed in the study.

claim: The association between goal-directed deficits and compulsive behavior/intrusive thought was highly specific when compared to other non-compulsive aspects of psychopathology.
source: This association was highly specific when compared to other non-compulsive aspects of psychopathology.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparisons in the study data.

claim: A deficit in deliberative, 'goal-directed' control may leave individuals vulnerable to rely excessively on forming more rigid habits.
source: In particular, a deficit in deliberative, 'goal-directed' control may leave individuals vulnerable to rely excessively on forming more rigid habits.
evidence: This claim is based on theoretical frameworks cited in the literature.

claim: Habits are behaviors that animals and humans learn to execute automatically when presented with familiar environmental cues.
source: Habits are behaviors that animals and humans learn to execute automatically when presented with familiar environmental cues (Dickinson, 1985).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dickinson, 1985.

claim: Habits cannot adapt flexibly to new situations.
source: While habits are typically very useful, allowing us to efficiently perform routine actions while expending minimal cognitive effort, they cannot adapt flexibly to new situations.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about habit formation.

claim: Goal-directed behavior refers to the ability to make more considered choices, reflecting both knowledge of the outcomes that actions typically produce and current motivation for those outcomes.
source: This refers our ability to make more considered choices, reflecting both (i) knowledge of the outcomes that our actions typically produce and (ii) our current motivation for those outcomes (Dickinson and Balleine, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dickinson and Balleine, 1994.

claim: Deficits in goal-directed learning have been observed across drug addiction.
source: Consistent with the hypothesis that compulsion is linked to an imbalance between these modes of control, deficits in goal-directed learning have been observed across a range of putatively compulsive disorders such as drug addiction (Sjoerds et al., 2013; Voon et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sjoerds et al., 2013 and Voon et al., 2015.

claim: Deficits in goal-directed learning have been observed in obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD).
source: obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) (Voon et al., 2015; Gillan et al., 2011; 2014a; 2014b; 2015a)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on OCD.

claim: Deficits in goal-directed learning have been observed in binge-eating disorder.
source: and also binge-eating disorder (Voon et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Voon et al., 2015.

claim: Deficits in goal-directed control have been linked to abnormal structure and function of the caudate and medial orbitofrontal cortex.
source: These deficits in goal-directed control have been linked to abnormal structure and function of the caudate and medial orbitofrontal cortex (Voon et al., 2015; Gillan et al., 2015a)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Voon et al., 2015 and Gillan et al., 2015a.

claim: A similar deficit in goal-directed control was reported in social anxiety disorder patients.
source: In fact, a similar deficit in goal-directed control was recently reported in other patient groups (Alvares et al., 2014; Morris et al., 2015), including those diagnosed with social anxiety disorder and schizophrenia
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Alvares et al., 2014 and Morris et al., 2015.

claim: A similar deficit in goal-directed control was reported in schizophrenia patients.
source: In fact, a similar deficit in goal-directed control was recently reported in other patient groups (Alvares et al., 2014; Morris et al., 2015), including those diagnosed with social anxiety disorder and schizophrenia
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Alvares et al., 2014 and Morris et al., 2015.

claim: There are high rates of co-morbidity between OCD and social anxiety disorder.
source: Of particular relevance to the present study are the high rates of co-morbidity between OCD and social anxiety disorder (Ruscio et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ruscio et al., 2010.

claim: There is a preponderance of OCD symptoms in the schizophrenia population.
source: the preponderance of OCD symptoms in the schizophrenia poopulation (Poyurovsky and Koran, 2005)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Poyurovsky and Koran, 2005.

claim: The vast majority of patients diagnosed with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) meet the criteria for another lifetime psychiatric disorder.
source: and more broadly that the vast majority of patients diagnosed with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) meet the criteria for another lifetime psychiatric disorder (Ruscio et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ruscio et al., 2010.

claim: The DSM was developed to provide a reliable, descriptive psychiatric taxonomy, rather than an etiologically valid one.
source: Indeed, the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM), now in it's fifth edition (American Psychiatric Association, 2013) was developed to provide a reliable, descriptive psychiatric taxonomy, rather than an etiologically valid one.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the DSM-5.

claim: It is difficult to clearly discriminate DSM diagnostic categories on the basis of genetics, neuroimaging, or modern tools of cognitive neuroscience.
source: As such it is difficult to clearly discriminate the diagnostic categories it defines on the basis of genetics, neuroimaging, or indeed any of the modern tools of cognitive neuroscience.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the descriptive nature of DSM categories.

claim: The National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH) has launched the Research Domain Criteria (RDoC) initiative, aiming to identify biologically plausible, trans-diagnostic markers of psychiatric disturbances.
source: These issues have been described in detail by others (Cuthbert and Kozak, 2013; Hyman, 2007; Robbins et al., 2012), and have been recognized by the National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH), which has launched the Research Domain Criteria (RDoC) initiative, aiming to identify biologically plausible, trans-diagnostic markers of psychiatric disturbances (Insel et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cuthbert and Kozak, 2013; Hyman, 2007; Robbins et al., 2012; and Insel et al., 2010.

claim: Model-based learning is a form of reinforcement learning that has been computationally formalized as arising from goal-directed control.
source: Goal-directed control has recently been computationally formalized as arising from a form of reinforcement learning known as 'model-based' (Daw et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Daw et al., 2011.

claim: Model-based learning can be expressed as an individual difference measure that has been shown to predict how likely individuals are to form habits.
source: which can be expressed as an individual difference measure that has been shown to predict how likely individuals are to form habits (Gillan et al., 2015c).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gillan et al., 2015c.

claim: In Experiment 1, total scores on a self-report questionnaire measuring the severity of OCD symptoms were tracked by normal variation in model-based learning in the general population.
source: In Experiment 1, we found that total scores on a self-report questionnaire measuring the severity of OCD symptoms were tracked by normal variation in model-based learning in the general population
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Experiment 1.

claim: In Experiment 1, self-report anxiety symptoms were not associated with model-based learning.
source: but not by self-report anxiety or depression symptoms.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Experiment 1.

claim: In Experiment 1, self-report depression symptoms were not associated with model-based learning.
source: but not by self-report anxiety or depression symptoms.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Experiment 1.

claim: In Experiment 2, the association between self-report OCD symptoms and model-based learning was replicated.
source: In Experiment 2, we replicated the association with self-report OCD symptoms
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Experiment 2.

claim: The association between OCD symptoms and goal-directed deficits generalized to alcohol addiction symptoms.
source: and showed that it generalized to a broader set of psychiatric symptoms that similarly involve failures in exerting control over self-deleterious behaviors, specifically alcohol addiction, eating disorders and impulsivity.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Experiment 2.

claim: The association between OCD symptoms and goal-directed deficits generalized to eating disorder symptoms.
source: and showed that it generalized to a broader set of psychiatric symptoms that similarly involve failures in exerting control over self-deleterious behaviors, specifically alcohol addiction, eating disorders and impulsivity.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Experiment 2.

claim: The association between OCD symptoms and goal-directed deficits generalized to impulsivity symptoms.
source: and showed that it generalized to a broader set of psychiatric symptoms that similarly involve failures in exerting control over self-deleterious behaviors, specifically alcohol addiction, eating disorders and impulsivity.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Experiment 2.

claim: Factor analysis indicated the existence of three latent symptom dimensions that cut across the nine different questionnaires assessed in this study.
source: Next, we conducted a factor analysis, which indicated the existence of three latent symptom dimensions that cut across the nine different questionnaires assessed in this study.
evidence: This claim is supported by factor analysis of the data.

claim: The second symptom dimension identified was characterized by 'Compulsive Behavior and Intrusive Thought', in which items were most consistently drawn from the questionnaires assessing symptoms of OCD, eating disorders and addiction.
source: Crucially, the second symptom dimension identified was characterized by 'Compulsive Behavior and Intrusive Thought', in which items were most consistently drawn from the questionnaires assessing symptoms of OCD, eating disorders and addiction, pertaining not just to repetitive compulsive behaviors (as was our prediction), but also to associated preoccupations and cognitive distortions.
evidence: This claim is supported by factor analysis of the data.

claim: The 'Compulsive Behavior and Intrusive Thought' factor was a significant predictor of deficits in model-based learning.
source: This factor, which was defined independently of task performance, was a significant predictor of deficits in model-based learning.
evidence: This claim is supported by regression analysis of the data.

claim: The effect of 'Compulsive Behavior and Intrusive Thought' on model-based learning was highly specific to this factor, when directly compared to the two other factors identified ('Anxious-Depression' and 'Social Withdrawal').
source: Crucially, this effect was highly specific to this factor, when directly compared to the two other factors identified in this analysis, 'Anxious-Depression' and 'Social Withdrawal'.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparisons in the data.

claim: In Experiment 1, participants (N = 548) were 357 females (65%) and 191 males with ages ranging from 18 to 72 (M=35, SD=11).
source: Participants in Experiment 1 (N=548) were 357 females (65%) and 191 males with ages ranging from 18 to 72 (M=35, SD=11).
evidence: This claim describes the demographic characteristics of the sample.

claim: In Experiment 2, participants (N=1413) were 823 females (58%) and 590 males with ages ranging from 18 to 76 (M=33, SD=11).
source: Experiment 2, participants (N=1413) were 823 females (58%) and 590 males with ages ranging from 18 to 76 (M=33, SD=11).
evidence: This claim describes the demographic characteristics of the sample.

claim: There was a significant association between scores on the OCD questionnaire and goal-directed deficits (β = −0.040, Standard Error (SE) = 0.02, p=0.049) when controlling for age, IQ and gender.
source: In line with our hypothesis, there was a significant association between scores on the OCD questionnaire and goal-directed deficits (i.e. a negative relationship between OCD severity and model-based learning; β = −0.040, Standard Error (SE) = 0.02, p=0.049) when (as in all analyses reported henceforth) controlling for age, IQ and gender, which have been previously reported to covary with goal-directed behavior (Eppinger et al., 2013; Schad et al., 2014; Sandstrom et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data from Experiment 1.

claim: For each increase of 1 standard deviation (SD) in the total score on the OCD questionnaire, model-based learning was reduced by 14%.
source: Specifically, for each increase of 1 standard deviation (SD) in the total score on the OCD questionnaire, model-based learning was reduced by 14%.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data from Experiment 1.

claim: No relationship was observed between self-report depression and model-based learning (β = −0.016, SE = 0.02, p=0.439).
source: No such relationship was observed for self-report depression (β = −0.016, SE = 0.02, p=0.439)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data from Experiment 1.

claim: No relationship was observed between trait anxiety and model-based learning (β = −0.006, SE = 0.02, p=0.777).
source: or trait anxiety (β = −0.006, SE = 0.02, p=0.777) severity (Table 1, Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data from Experiment 1.

claim: The relationship between total scores on the OCD questionnaire and goal-directed deficits survived inclusion of the depression and trait anxiety total scores in the same model as covariates (β = −0.048, SE = 0.02, p=0.04).
source: Moreover, the relationship between total scores on the OCD questionnaire and goal-directed deficits survived inclusion of the depression and trait anxiety total scores in the same model as covariates (β = −0.048, SE = 0.02, p=0.04).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data from Experiment 1.

claim: Deficits in goal-directed control are a marker of normal variation in OCD symptomatology in the general population.
source: These data indicate that deficits in goal-directed control are a marker of normal variation in OCD symptomatology in the general population.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the data from Experiment 1.

claim: In Experiment 2, scores on the OCD questionnaire were significantly associated with goal-directed deficits (β=−0.026, SE=0.01, p=0.020), while controlling for age, gender and IQ.
source: In this independent sample, we replicated the results from Experiment 1; scores on the OCD questionnaire were significantly associated with goal-directed deficits (β=−0.026, SE=0.01, p=0.020), while controlling for age, gender and IQ (Table 1, Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data from Experiment 2.

claim: Total scores on self-report measures of eating disorder severity were associated with goal-directed deficits (β=−0.037, SE=0.01, p<0.001).
source: As we hypothesized, this effect generalized to phenotypically disparate manifestations of psychiatric compulsivity: total scores on self-report measures of eating disorder severity (β=−0.037, SE=0.01, p<0.001)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data from Experiment 2.

claim: Total scores on self-report measures of impulsivity were associated with goal-directed deficits (β=−0.034, SE=0.01, p=0.007).
source: impulsivity (β=−0.034, SE=0.01, p=0.007)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data from Experiment 2.

claim: Total scores on self-report measures of alcohol addiction were associated with goal-directed deficits (β=−0.025, SE=0.01, p=0.029).
source: and alcohol addiction (β=−0.025, SE=0.01, p=0.029).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data from Experiment 2.

claim: No significant associations were found between goal-directed deficits and total scores on the depression questionnaire (β=−0.01, SE=0.01, p=0.385).
source: Also as predicted, we found no significant associations between goal-directed deficits and total scores on the depression (β=−0.01, SE=0.01, p=0.385)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data from Experiment 2.

claim: No significant associations were found between goal-directed deficits and total scores on the apathy questionnaire (β=−0.001, SE=0.01, p=0.953).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data from Experiment 2.

claim: No significant associations were found between goal-directed deficits and total scores on the trait anxiety questionnaire (β=−0.008, SE=0.01, p=0.498).
source: trait anxiety (β=−0.008, SE=0.01, p=0.498)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data from Experiment 2.

claim: No significant associations were found between goal-directed deficits and total scores on the social anxiety questionnaire (β=0.008, SE=0.01, p=0.496).
source: or social anxiety (β=0.008, SE=0.01, p=0.496) questionnaires.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data from Experiment 2.

claim: No significant association was found between self-report levels of schizotypy and goal-directed control (β=−0.017, SE=0.01, p=0.14).
source: We found no significant association between self-report levels of schizotypy and goal-directed control (β=−0.017, SE=0.01, p=0.14), possibly reflective of the great deal of heterogeneity within this particular psychiatric construct.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data from Experiment 2.

claim: 'Compulsive Behavior and Intrusive Thought' had high and consistent loadings from almost all items pertaining to eating disorders (Mean loading=0.36, SD=0.15).
source: Although the labeling of factors is of course a subjective process, quantitatively speaking, 'Compulsive Behavior and Intrusive Thought' had high and consistent loadings from almost all items pertaining to eating disorders (Mean loading=0.36, SD=0.15)
evidence: This claim is supported by factor analysis of the data.

claim: 'Compulsive Behavior and Intrusive Thought' had high and consistent loadings from almost all items pertaining to OCD (Mean loading=0.50, SD=0.06).
source: OCD (Mean loading=0.50, SD=0.06)
evidence: This claim is supported by factor analysis of the data.

claim: 'Compulsive Behavior and Intrusive Thought' had high and consistent loadings from almost all items pertaining to addiction (Mean loading=0.31, SD=0.07).
source: and addiction (Mean loading=0.31, SD=0.07)
evidence: This claim is supported by factor analysis of the data.

claim: Items from the impulsivity scale did not load as strongly or consistently on the 'Compulsive Behavior and Intrusive Thought' factor (M=0.15, SD=0.15) compared to eating disorders, OCD, and addiction items.
source: Items from the impulsivity scale (of which the total score was a significant predictor of goal-directed deficits) did not load as strongly or consistently on this factor (M=0.15, SD=0.15; significantly less than the former three questionnaires, Eating Disorders vs. Impulsivity: t(52)=5.178; OCD vs. Impulsivity: t(41)=11.379; Alcohol Addiction vs. Impulsivity: t(33)=4.342, all p<0.001) (Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of factor loadings.

claim: When tested alone, 'Compulsive Behavior and Intrusive Thought' was significantly associated with deficits in goal-directed learning (β=−0.046, SE=0.01, p<0.001).
source: When tested alone, 'Compulsive Behavior and Intrusive Thought' was significantly associated with deficits in goal-directed learning (β=−0.046, SE=0.01, p<0.001)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: The effect size of 'Compulsive Behavior and Intrusive Thought' on model-based learning was greater than that of any of the questionnaires used in this study, corresponding to a 17% reduction in model-based learning for an increase of 1 SD in 'Compulsive Behavior and Intrusive Thought'.
source: and this effect size was greater than that of any of the questionnaires used in this study, corresponding to a 17% reduction in model-based learning for an increase of 1 SD in 'Compulsive Behavior and Intrusive Thought' (Figure 3B, Table 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: There were no significant effects of Factor 1 ('Anxious-Depression') on model-based learning (β=−0.001, (0.01), p=0.92).
source: There were no significant effects of Factor 1 (β=−0.001, (0.01), p=0.92)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: There were no significant effects of Factor 3 ('Social Withdrawal') on model-based learning (β=0.013, SE=0.01, p=0.24).
source: or Factor 3 (β=0.013, SE=0.01, p=0.24) on model-based learning.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Deficits in goal-directed control were highly specific to the 'Compulsive Behavior and Intrusive Thought' factor versus 'Anxious-Depression' (β=−0.062, SE=0.02, p=0.001).
source: We found that deficits in goal-directed control were highly specific to the 'Compulsive Behavior and Intrusive Thought' (vs. 'Anxious-Depression', β=−0.062, SE=0.02, p=0.001
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparisons in the data.

claim: Deficits in goal-directed control were highly specific to the 'Compulsive Behavior and Intrusive Thought' factor versus 'Social Withdrawal' (β=−0.089, SE=0.02, p<0.001).
source: vs. 'Social Withdrawal', β=−0.089, SE=0.02, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparisons in the data.

claim: When included in the same model with the other factors, 'Social Withdrawal' emerged as a significant positive predictor of goal-directed control over action (β=0.031, SE=0.01, p=0.014).
source: Moreover, when included in the same model with the other factors, 'Social Withdrawal' (onto which addiction and aspects of impulsivity load negatively) emerged as a significant positive predictor of goal-directed control over action (β=0.031, SE=0.01, p=0.014).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: There was no evidence for nonlinearity in the relationship between goal-directed deficits and 'Compulsive Behavior and Intrusive Thought' (beta=−0.0016, p=0.822).
source: We found no evidence for nonlinearity (beta=−0.0016, p=0.822)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis testing for quadratic effects.

claim: The linear effect of 'Compulsive Behavior and Intrusive Thought' on goal-directed deficits remained significant when a quadratic term was included in the model (beta=−0.045, p=0.001).
source: and the linear effect remained significant when included in this model (beta=−0.045, p=0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis testing for quadratic effects.

claim: Model-free performance on the learning task did not track any of the scores from psychiatric questionnaires.
source: First, although individual variation in 'model-free' performance on the learning task did not track any of the scores from our psychiatric questionnaires (Supplementary file 1C)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: In Experiment 1, model-free performance related significantly to age (Reward*Age interaction).
source: in Experiment 1, model-free performance did relate significantly to age (Supplementary file 1B, Reward*Age interaction).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data from Experiment 1.

claim: Higher IQ was associated with increases in goal-directed, 'model-based' learning.
source: In particular, higher IQ was associated with increases in goal-directed, 'model-based' learning.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Older people were significantly less 'model-based' compared to their younger counterparts.
source: In contrast to the effect of age on 'model-free' learning, older people were significantly less 'model-based' compared to their younger counterparts.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Males were significantly less model-free relative to females tested in this study.
source: Males were significantly less model-free and more model-based relative to females tested in this study.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data from Experiment 2.

claim: Males were significantly more model-based relative to females tested in this study.
source: Males were significantly less model-free and more model-based relative to females tested in this study.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data from Experiment 2.

claim: Self-report scores of OCD and addiction symptoms being associated with goal-directed deficits is consistent with previous research in patient populations.
source: That self-report scores of OCD and addiction symptoms were associated with these deficits is consistent with previous research in patient populations (Sjoerds et al., 2013; Voon et al., 2015; Gillan et al., 2011; 2014a; 2014b; 2015a)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The present study extends findings on OCD and addiction to a general population sample for the first time.
source: and extends these results for the first time to a general population sample.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the novelty of the current study's findings.

claim: Binge-eating disorder has been previously associated with reduced goal-directed control in one patient study and an animal model.
source: Likewise, binge-eating disorder has also been previously associated with reduced goal-directed control in one patient study and an animal model (Voon et al., 2015; Furlong et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Voon et al., 2015 and Furlong et al., 2014.

claim: The present study extends the finding on binge-eating disorder to self-report symptoms of other subtypes of eating disorders.
source: Critically, the results of the present study extend this finding to self-report symptoms of other subtypes of eating disorders
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the novelty of the current study's findings.

claim: Compulsive Behavior and Intrusive Thought (and associated deficits in goal-directed control) are a key component of more aspects of eating disorders than previously documented.
source: suggesting that Compulsive Behavior and Intrusive Thought (and associated deficits in goal-directed control) are a key component of more aspects of eating disorders than previously documented.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Items relating to exerting control over food intake (e.g. 'I display self-control around food') did not load strongly on the 'Compulsive Behavior and Intrusive Thought' factor.
source: An entirely consistent exception was that items relating to exerting control over food intake (e.g. "I display self-control around food") did not load strongly on the 'Compulsive Behavior and Intrusive Thought' factor.
evidence: This claim is supported by factor analysis of the data.

claim: A previous study reported an association between social anxiety disorder and deficits in goal-directed control.
source: A previous study reported an association between social anxiety disorder and deficits in goal-directed control (Alvares et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Alvares et al., 2014.

claim: Using self-report social anxiety symptom scores in the general population sample, the present study did not replicate the finding of an association with goal-directed deficits.
source: Using self-report social anxiety symptom scores in our general population sample, we did not replicate this finding
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: The present study observed a trend towards enhanced goal-directed control associated with social anxiety symptoms.
source: and in fact observed a trend towards enhanced goal-directed control associated with social anxiety symptoms.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Schizophrenia has been previously associated with deficits in goal-directed control.
source: Schizophrenia has also been previously associated with deficits in goal-directed control (Morris et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Morris et al., 2015.

claim: The present study did not find a significant association between the total score on the schizotypy questionnaire and deficits in goal-directed control.
source: Consistent with the heterogeneous nature of schizophrenia, where two diagnosed patients can have entirely non-overlapping symptoms (American Psychological Association, 2013), we did not find a significant association between the total score on the schizotypy questionnaire and deficits in goal-directed control (although this was significant in a second analysis based on a full computational model).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Using the trans-diagnostic approach, 'unusual experiences' characteristic of schizotypy loaded onto the 'Compulsive Behavior and Intrusive Thought' factor.
source: However, using our trans-diagnostic approach, we found that in particular 'unusual experiences' characteristic of schizotypy loaded onto the 'Compulsive Behavior and Intrusive Thought' factor, which in turn was a strong predictor of goal-directed deficits.
evidence: This claim is supported by factor analysis of the data.

claim: Delusions are more closely linked to executive deficits than the negative symptoms of schizophrenia.
source: This finding converges with studies highlighting that delusions are more closely linked to executive deficits than the negative symptoms of schizophrenia (Lysaker et al., 1998; 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lysaker et al., 1998 and 2003.

claim: Schizophrenia and OCD share a common pattern of abnormal beliefs.
source: In terms of clinical phenomenology, schizophrenia and OCD share a common pattern of abnormal beliefs and as DSM-5 and others have noted, the distinction between a delusion in schizophrenia and a strongly held belief in OCD is often blurred (Poyurovsky and Koran, 2005; American Psychological Association, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Poyurovsky and Koran, 2005 and the DSM-5.

claim: 'Compulsive Behavior and Intrusive Thought' may be common to both schizophrenia and OCD and explained by deficits in goal-directed control.
source: These data suggest that 'Compulsive Behavior and Intrusive Thought', which comprises automatic behaviors as well as associated repetitive thoughts, may be common to both schizophrenia and OCD and explained by deficits in goal-directed control.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Earlier work investigating deficits in goal-directed learning in compulsive patient populations did not employ a positive clinical control.
source: Earlier work investigating deficits in goal-directed learning in compulsive patient populations did not employ a positive clinical control (Voon et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Voon et al., 2015.

claim: Prior studies have found a consistent association between stress and goal-directed learning deficits.
source: For instance, prior studies have found a consistent association between stress and goal-directed learning deficits (Otto et al., 2013; Schwabe and Wolf, 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Otto et al., 2013 and Schwabe and Wolf, 2009.

claim: The present study found no association between 'Anxious-Depression' and deficits in goal-directed control.
source: Here, we tested this possibility rigorously in two independent samples. We found no association between 'Anxious-Depression' and deficits in goal-directed control
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: The specificity of goal-directed deficits to 'Compulsive Behavior and Intrusive Thought' was confirmed through direct statistical comparisons.
source: and moreover the specificity of goal-directed deficits to 'Compulsive Behavior and Intrusive Thought' was confirmed through direct statistical comparisons.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparisons in the data.

claim: Prior work has shown that model-based learning deficits predict the presence of habits using a devaluation probe.
source: Prior work has shown that the model-based learning deficits predict the presence of habits using a devaluation probe (Gillan et al., 2015c)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gillan et al., 2015c.

claim: When OCD patients are performing habits, they show dysfunctional hyperactivity in the caudate.
source: Indeed, this converges with prior work showing that when OCD patients are performing habits, they show dysfunctional hyperactivity in the caudate (Gillan et al., 2015a)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gillan et al., 2015a.

claim: The caudate is a region associated with goal-directed control over behavior.
